1. The animation shows how inflation wears down the buying power of a fixed income payment. Its illustrative retiree, Carl, starts in January 1966 with a first check worth 10 crates of goods. His check grows only about 2% a year, while prices rise 6.38% a year, which the animation calls the fastest stretch.

2. Prices, shown as a rising blue bar, go up much faster than Carl's check. The row of 10 crates that his check can buy fades out one by one. By year 13 about half the crates are gone, and by year 20 only about 4 of the 10 are left. A small chart in frame 6 shows a second person, Ruth, whose buying power was back above its starting level in the early years.

3. A check that grows slowly, or not at all, buys less and less as prices rise. In this example Carl had less buying power on all 20 of 20 anniversaries. The labels "ILLUSTRATIVE" and "US only · history, not a forecast" say it is a historical example, not a prediction.

4. A viewer might take away that a payout which doesn't keep up with inflation can lose a lot of value over a long retirement. As a 64-year-old comparing two payout options, I'd look at whether either one adjusts for inflation, and at how the starting payment compares with how it grows. The frames don't tell me which option to pick.

5. The animation didn't state this advice. It only shows the loss of buying power under one historical stretch of high inflation, so the link to choosing between annuity options is my own conclusion.
